plan.contextChunk: This figure is a line graph with two smooth curves showing how the equilibrium composition of a two-isomer mixture depends on the energy difference between the isomers. The plotting field is pale blue with a faint grid. The vertical axis is labeled Percent and runs from 0 to 100 with labels every 20 units. The same horizontal variable is given two scales: the bottom axis, labeled Energy difference (kJ/mol), extends from 0 to 15 with labeled ticks at 5, 10 and 15, while the top axis, labeled Energy difference (kcal/mol), covers 0 to just over 3 with ticks at 0, 1, 2 and 3. Both curves originate together at 50 percent where the energy difference is zero. The blue curve, tagged by a curved leader line to the label More stable isomer, rises steeply at small energy differences and then flattens, passing roughly 90 percent near 6 kJ/mol and approaching 100 percent at the right edge. The magenta curve, similarly tagged Less stable isomer, is its mirror image, dropping steeply and then leveling out at a few percent. The two curves add to 100 at every horizontal position, so a vertical slice anywhere on the plot reads off the population split for that energy gap. The graph attaches numbers to the relationship between a modest energy separation and a strongly lopsided equilibrium mixture.

interactionPlan.concept: At equilibrium, the population split between two isomers is set by their energy difference through the Boltzmann/Gibbs relation, so even a small energy gap (a few kJ/mol) produces a strongly lopsided mixture.
elements: Pale blue plotting field with faint horizontal and vertical grid lines
Left y-axis labeled 'Percent', range 0-100, ticks every 20
Bottom x-axis labeled 'Energy difference (kJ/mol)', range 0-15, labeled ticks at 5, 10, 15 with minor ticks every 1
Top x-axis labeled 'Energy difference (kcal/mol)', range 0 to ~3.4, labeled ticks at 0, 1, 2, 3 (aligned to the same physical variable, 1 kcal = 4.184 kJ)
Blue (teal) curve rising from 50% at 0 kJ/mol toward ~99% at 14 kJ/mol — percentage of the more stable isomer
Magenta curve falling from 50% at 0 kJ/mol toward ~1% at 14 kJ/mol — percentage of the less stable isomer
Curved leader-line annotation pointing to the blue curve labeled 'More stable isomer'
Curved leader-line annotation pointing to the magenta curve labeled 'Less stable isomer'
Shared starting point marker at (0 kJ/mol, 50%) where both curves meet
Interactive vertical guide line at the selected energy difference
Readout box showing current energy (in selected units), more-stable %, less-stable %, and their sum = 100%
Two dot markers where the guide line intersects each curve
Optional stacked bar mini-panel showing the population split as filled fractions

interactions.label: Energy difference ΔE (kJ/mol)
interactions.teaches: That the two isomer percentages always sum to 100 and that the split swings from even to overwhelmingly one-sided over just a few kJ/mol.

interactions.label: Cursor energy units
interactions.teaches: That the two horizontal scales are the same physical quantity in different units — the vertical slice and the percentages do not move when the unit changes.

demo_steps.title: No energy difference: a 50:50 mixture
demo_steps.narration: With ΔE = 0 the two isomers are equally stable, so the curves meet at 50 percent. Neither form is favored at equilibrium.

demo_steps.title: A small gap already tips the balance
demo_steps.narration: Slide to about 2 kJ/mol — less than the energy of a weak interaction — and the mixture is already roughly 70:30. Tiny energy differences have outsized population consequences.

demo_steps.title: The classic 95:5 split
demo_steps.narration: Near 7.5 kJ/mol the more stable isomer accounts for about 95 percent of the mixture. This is the region where chemists start calling a conformer 'strongly preferred'.

demo_steps.title: Same slice, different units
demo_steps.narration: Switch the readout to kcal/mol: the guide line does not move and the percentages are unchanged — 7.5 kJ/mol is simply 1.8 kcal/mol. The top and bottom axes describe one relationship.

demo_steps.title: Diminishing returns at large ΔE
demo_steps.narration: Push toward 12-14 kJ/mol and the less stable isomer drops below one percent; the curves flatten, so extra stability buys very little additional population.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Equilibrium population depends exponentially on energy, so an energy gap smaller than a single weak bond — only a few kJ/mol — already makes the mixture roughly 95:5 rather than 50:50.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Single panel line plot with a pale blue (#e6f3fa) plot field and faint gray grid. Y-axis 'Percent' 0-100, ticks every 20. Bottom x-axis 'Energy difference (kJ/mol)' 0-15 with labeled ticks at 5, 10, 15; top x-axis 'Energy difference (kcal/mol)' 0-3.4 with labeled ticks at 0,1,2,3, both mapped to the same underlying variable (kcal = kJ/4.184). Two smooth curves both starting at (0, 50): a teal/steel-blue curve rising concavely to ~99% at the right edge, and a magenta/crimson curve that is its exact mirror about the 50% line, falling to ~1%. Curves follow the Boltzmann form: more stable % = 100/(1+exp(-ΔE/RT)) with RT ≈ 2.48 kJ/mol at 298 K. Annotate the blue curve with a thin curved arrow from the right-center to text 'More stable isomer', and the magenta curve with a similar curved arrow to 'Less stable isomer' in the lower right. Interactive layer: a dark vertical guide line at the slider value with filled circular markers at each curve intersection, plus a small readout panel near the top-right showing energy in the toggled unit and both percentages with a '= 100%' sum note. Keep text in a clean sans-serif; label color matches its curve.

authoredContext:
You might recall from your general chemistry course that it’s possible to calculate the percentages of two isomers at equilibrium using the equation ΔE = –RT ln K, where ΔE is the energy difference between isomers, R is the gas constant [8.315 J/(K·mol)], T is the Kelvin temperature, and K is the equilibrium constant between isomers. For example, an energy difference of 7.6 kJ/mol means that about 95% of methylcyclohexane molecules have an equatorial methyl group at any given instant while only 5% have an axial methyl group. The figure plots the relationship between energy and isomer percentages.

A plot of the percentages of two isomers at equilibrium versus the energy difference between them. The curves are calculated using the equation ΔE = −RT ln K.

A graph of percent against energy difference in kilojoules per mole plots an increasing curve for more stable isomer and decreasing curve for less stable isomer.

The energy difference between axial and equatorial conformations is due to steric strain caused by 1,3-diaxial interactions. The axial methyl group on C1 is too close to the axial hydrogens three carbons away on C3 and C5, resulting in 7.6 kJ/mol of steric strain (the figure).

discrepancies: The light-blue plot field in the source stops where the data ends (~14 kJ/mol), leaving a thin white strip before the right border at 15; the generated version fills the entire plot rectangle out to 15.

The two annotation labels sit slightly further left/inside the plot than in the source (source places 'More stable isomer' starting near x≈11 and 'Less stable isomer' near x≈10.5, closer to the right border), and the leader arrows are a bit shorter/less curved than the original hand-drawn arcs.

Bottom-axis minor ticks at every 1 kJ/mol are rendered, but the source's tick marks are drawn outside the axis with a slightly heavier weight; the generated ticks are shorter and lighter — a cosmetic difference only.

The generated blue curve appears to reach the 100 % gridline visually near x≈12, whereas the source curve is visibly a hair below 100 across the whole plateau (both are correct numerically, but the source reads as asymptotic).
